Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Rapid computations of spectrotemporal prediction error support perception of degraded speech" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Andrew King (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been greatly improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

1) The new analyses performed in response to point 3 revealed that the main result of the paper, an interaction between match/mismatch and sensory detail, is also present in a null distribution of their data. The authors offer a potential explanation, but admit that they do not fully understand this result. This seems concerning; if the main result of their study is also present in a control analysis with shuffled trial labels, it is unclear how to interpret these effects. Given the impact of this finding on the interpretability of the results, it does not seem appropriate to omit these results from the manuscript. We recommend including these findings in the paper, along with the (admittedly speculative, but plausible) explanation offered by the authors. Note that this refers specifically to the results of the null distribution analysis of the main results, the reviewers agree with the authors that it's fine to omit the more speculative “written mismatch” analysis (i.e., using the acoustic representation of a word they didn't actually hear) suggested by the reviewers in the previous round.

2) The authors point out how they think they obtained their results because MEG is more sensitive to error unit than hypothesis unit processing. If this was a general rule, two visual MEG studies by Kok and colleagues (2017 PNAS; 2020 J Neurosci) would be unlikely to have found these sharpening patterns. Could the authors say anything about this discrepancy? Is it perhaps more plausible that these auditory data, in combination with the visual findings, might suggest a difference between visual and auditory systems in the extent to which MEG reflects hypothesis v error processing?

3) Relatedly, the authors have interestingly added a time resolved analysis. Given the interaction is seen very early, they consider this finding less consistent with the opposing process account (Press et al., 2020). However, the opposing process account describes perception, and in terms of neural processing is proposed to be reflected in hypothesis unit processing, not error unit processing. If the authors believe they are seeing the processing in error units only in their study, the data do not in fact speak to the opposing process account. If our understanding of the authors' claims is correct, we would suggest amending the paragraph that mentions this account – mentioning that it's a theory of perception and more concerned with hypothesis unit processing which is hypothesised not to be reflected in the present data.

4) The authors have increased clarity concerning how the predictive coding account could explain the present dataset – by clarifying the assumed precision of the priors. However, the reviewers felt the fact that there is greater representation of matching 3 channel than non-matching 3 channel under this account could still be explained more clearly. It was not fully clear how the clarifications provided speak to this particular point. E.g, if assuming a precise gaussian prediction for clay, an imprecise gaussian with the same mean (clay) will overlap with that gaussian more than an imprecise gaussian with a different mean (fast). Higher Kullback Leibler divergence for mismatch still i.e., by prescribing the shape of the prior, they have accounted for why 3 channel can generate more error than 12 channel, but not relative differences between match and non-match in the 3 channel. We think it would help readers if the logic could be further clarified here as our conceptualisation of error processing may deviate from the authors'.

5) With respect to the discussion of the lack of correspondence to the Broderick findings – this may be due to the fact that the Broderick paper was based on semantic similarity – which is not the same thing as predictability. Indeed, Frank and Willems (2017) found that semantic similarity and semantic surprisal were not strongly correlated with each other. It may even be that the Broderick results based on semantic similarity map better onto the earlier activity from hypothesis units and do not tap into error unit activity as much (which might be accessible by exploring the top-down role of semantic surprisal).

6) We don't insist on making changes necessarily – but the transition from the "Stimulus feature space selection" subsection to the "Acoustic analysis…" subsection (p12 – 13) still seems a little weak. You have just spent a lot of time comparing models and then quite quickly converge on the spectrotemporal one. You attempt to justify it might best match with the vocoded speech – but might not that actually work against you? The idea is that you are hoping to be sensitive to error, no? So if you have a strong prior and then get a degraded speech input, don't you want to be sensitive to the details of that prior – and, hence, the error. Again, we don't insist on any major change here. It may suffice that you just wanted to keep the story fairly straightforward and so wanted to pick the single speech representation that performed best.

results.result: The study included 21 right-handed, native English-speaking participants aged 18-40 years (mean=22, SD=2) with no self-reported hearing impairment or neurological disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 provide clear demographic and inclusion criteria for the participant sample. These are standard methodological details that are explicitly stated and internally consistent.

results.result: The study used 468 monosyllabic words that were noise-vocoded with 3, 6, or 12 spectral channels to parametrically manipulate sensory detail while preserving temporal envelope information.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C10 describe the stimulus generation and vocoding procedure in detail. The technical specifications are clearly stated, the vocoding method is well-established (Shannon et al., 1995), and the parameters are appropriate for manipulating speech intelligibility.

results.result: Spectrotemporal modulation features best predicted MEG responses compared to envelope, spectrogram, and phonetic features, with sensor distributions consistent with bilateral superior temporal cortex sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 report the primary encoding model comparison with statistical support (post-hoc t-tests, Figure 3A) and anatomically plausible sensor topography (Figure 3B). The finding is robust and clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Speech spectrotemporal modulations show a lowpass profile following a 1/f relationship, with different modulation frequencies corresponding to distinct phonetic features (fast/broad for consonant bursts, slow/narrow for vowels, intermediate for formant transitions).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 characterize the acoustic properties of the stimuli with support from established literature. The 1/f relationship (C20) and phonetic interpretations (C21-C23) are well-documented in prior work and appropriately cited.

results.result: Increasing vocoder channels from 3 to 12 significantly enhanced intermediate spectrotemporal modulations (1-2 cycles/octave, 2-4 Hz) that are known to support speech intelligibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 report FDR-corrected statistical effects (Figure 4C) linking vocoding manipulation to specific acoustic changes. The connection to intelligibility is well-supported by multiple citations and consistent with the behavioral manipulation.

results.result: Neural encoding of spectrotemporal modulations showed a significant interaction between prior knowledge and sensory detail: matching text enhanced encoding for low-clarity speech but suppressed it for high-clarity speech, consistent with prediction error rather than sharpening.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 report the critical interaction effect with appropriate statistics (t-tests with effect sizes) in the left hemisphere. The pattern directly tests the theoretical prediction and is inconsistent with sharpening models (Figure 1D comparison). This is the study's central finding.

results.result: Even in conditions with lowest model accuracy (mismatching 3-channel and matching 12-channel), neural responses encoded spectrotemporal modulations significantly above chance as determined by feature-shuffled null distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 report permutation testing results (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) showing all conditions exceed chance (p<0.01). This control analysis confirms that neural encoding occurs even when the interaction reduces model accuracy.

results.result: Temporal response functions showed peaks at 87.5 and 150 ms, indicating that spectrotemporal modulation encoding occurs at short latencies consistent with early hierarchical processing stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 report TRF analysis results (Figure 5B) with clear temporal peaks. The interpretation that these short latencies reflect early processing is reasonable and consistent with the MEG literature, though the hierarchical inference is somewhat indirect.

results.result: Decoding analysis revealed that intermediate temporal modulations (2-4 Hz) were best represented in MEG responses, and the interaction between prior knowledge and sensory detail was specific to these intermediate modulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 report decoding results with FDR correction (Figure 6A-B). The finding that intermediate modulations are preferentially encoded is consistent with prior neurophysiology (multiple citations in C41), and the specificity of the interaction strengthens the main result.

results.result: Single-lag decoding analysis showed that the interaction between prior knowledge and sensory detail emerged rapidly, peaking around 50 ms after speech input.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 reports the temporal dynamics of the interaction effect (Figure 6D). The 50 ms peak timing is clearly shown in the data, though statistical significance is noted as marginal for some contrasts. This addresses a key question about when prediction errors are computed.

results.result: The study demonstrates four main findings: (1) spectrotemporal modulations best predict MEG responses, (2) intermediate modulations (2-4 Hz, 1-2 cycles/octave) distinguish words and are affected by vocoding, (3) prior knowledge and signal quality interactively influence neural representations peaking at ~50 ms, and (4) this interaction is specific to intermediate modulations, consistent with prediction error rather than sharpening.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C50 summarize the four main findings, each supported by the preceding analyses. The integration of encoding, acoustic, and decoding analyses provides converging evidence. The interpretation favoring prediction error over sharpening is well-justified by the interaction pattern.

results.result: Spectrotemporal modulations capture linguistically relevant features (formant transitions, fundamental frequency) and are well-represented in auditory cortex neurons as demonstrated by animal electrophysiology and human neuroimaging studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 contextualize the findings within established literature. All statements are appropriately cited and represent accurate summaries of prior work. This provides theoretical grounding for why spectrotemporal modulations are a meaningful feature space.

results.result: Cortical responses are selectively tuned to intermediate spectrotemporal modulations that convey speech information rather than faithfully encoding all acoustic detail, suggesting superior temporal neurons occupy an intermediate hierarchical stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 interpret the selective encoding of intermediate modulations. The inference is well-supported by the decoding results (C40) and consistent with cited literature. The hierarchical interpretation is reasonable given the partial acoustic invariance.

results.result: The interaction between sensory detail and prior knowledge provides unambiguous support for prediction error coding, and the rapid emergence within 100 ms indicates prediction errors are computed during early feedforward processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 draw strong theoretical conclusions from the interaction effect and its timing. The logic is sound: the interaction pattern uniquely distinguishes prediction error from sharpening (Blank & Davis 2016), and the early timing rules out late feedback-dependent mechanisms.

results.result: The experimental manipulation approach used here (varying both predictions and sensory quality) more clearly distinguishes prediction error from sharpening compared to natural listening paradigms where predictability measures are correlated.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 discuss methodological advantages and relate findings to other approaches. The argument that experimental control enables clearer theoretical tests is valid, and the discussion of semantic similarity vs. predictability (C65-C66) addresses potential conflicts with other studies.

results.result: The findings challenge TRACE-like models where prior knowledge only sharpens input, instead supporting predictive coding frameworks where prediction errors update higher-level representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 discuss theoretical implications. The challenge to TRACE is justified by the interaction pattern, and the support for predictive coding is appropriate. The caveat (C69) that prediction errors serve to update predictions (not as end representations) shows nuanced understanding.

results.result: Sharpened predictions may not be apparent in MEG data because they could reside in deeper cortical layers with lower MEG sensitivity or be communicated via distinct oscillatory channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 offer speculative explanations for why sharpened predictions weren't observed. While the hypotheses are plausible and appropriately cited, they remain untested. This is acknowledged as speculation and suggests future directions.

results.result: MEG data were acquired using a 204-channel VectorView system, with analysis restricted to planar gradiometers due to their superior sensitivity to local cortical sources and reduced noise susceptibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 describe MEG acquisition and preprocessing. The sensor selection rationale (C73) is well-justified and cited. Standard preprocessing steps (SSS, filtering, downsampling) are appropriate and clearly described.

results.result: Ridge regression encoding models mapped speech features to MEG responses using lags from -100 to 300 ms (predictions from 0-250 ms), with z-scored data and zero-padding to handle word boundaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 detail the encoding analysis methodology. The approach is standard in the field (multiple citations), preprocessing steps are appropriate, and the lag selection rationale (avoiding edge artifacts) is sound.

results.result: Decoding models used PCA-reduced MEG data (50 components) with ridge regression, optimizing lambda via leave-one-trial-out cross-validation and selecting the mode across participants and conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 describe decoding methodology. PCA dimensionality reduction is reasonable for computational efficiency, cross-validation is appropriate, and the lambda optimization strategy (mode selection, banded ridge for combined models) follows established practices.

results.result: Statistical testing used sensor selection (top 20 per hemisphere), permutation-based null distributions (feature-shuffled and word-shuffled), and DSS visualization of TRFs retaining the three most consistent components.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 describe statistical and visualization methods. Sensor selection is data-driven, permutation testing provides appropriate null distributions, and DSS is a standard method for visualizing TRFs. All approaches are well-justified.
